The B frames are composed and alive. They have dense, weathered materials (rust, grime, painted signage, car paint), clutter and life everywhere (vehicles, people, utilities, foliage), and real atmospheric depth (warm haze toward the sun, a skyline fading with distance, clouds with real volume). Two of them genuinely impress: the golden-hour backlight in pair 1 and the gritty liquor-store shot in pair 3. The A frames share four gaps that recur in every shot. (1) Surfaces are clean and unweathered (uniform paver grids, spotless walls), and the foregrounds are large empty stretches of road or pavement. (2) Landmarks look like placeholders: pink and white wireframe Supertrees and observation wheel, towers that are extruded boxes with window textures, and untextured boxes. (3) The lighting is pleasant but generic. There is no haze over distance and little contact shadow or ambient occlusion, the light reads as midday even when the description says late afternoon or warm sun, and the clouds look flat and 2D. (4) Every shot is framed around a centred vanishing point with nothing in the foreground to anchor it. The A frames' strongest assets are the shophouse modelling, the rain trees and the sky colour. Two caveats for the workflow. First, the test is not fully blind: B in pairs 1 and 2 carries a visible 'Grand Theft Auto V' logo, and the same Singapore-styled project sits in slot A in all four pairs, so the slot order is not randomised. Second, the B frames are curated marketing stills with posed heroes and tilted angles, while the A frames are eye-level captures, so the pairs are not like-for-like. Neither issue changes any verdict here, because the gaps are large.
